hero.eyebrow: An embeddable dynamic language for Rust
hero.headline: Scripting that feels like Rust.
hero.lead: Rune gives your Rust application a fast, async-first scripting language with the syntax your team already knows. Embed it in a few lines, then let your users program it.

features.title: Looks like Rust
features.text: Structs, enums, pattern matching, closures, modules and the ? operator, without types to annotate or a borrow checker to satisfy.

features.title: Async from the start
features.text: Async functions, closures and blocks, select, generators and streams are part of the language, and the host awaits a script like any other future.

features.title: Embeds cleanly
features.text: Expose Rust functions and types through a Module, call into scripts with vm.call, convert values with serde, and reload scripts while the host keeps running.

features.title: Limits the host controls
features.text: Instruction budgets, memory limits and a bounded compiler keep a script within what its host allows, on the way to a full sandbox.

features.title: Compact and fast
features.text: Scripts compile to a compact representation for a stack-based virtual machine, constants are evaluated at compile time, and a compiled unit can run on many threads at once.

features.title: Tooling included
features.text: The rune CLI comes with a language server, a formatter, a documentation generator and a test runner, and there is an extension for VS Code.

examples.title: Pattern matching
examples.text: Enums with data, guards and destructuring. If you can read Rust, you can already read Rune.

examples.title: Generators
examples.text: A function which yields is a generator: an infinite sequence, computed only as far as it is used.

examples.title: Closures & iterators
examples.text: Closures capture their environment, and iterators chain the way they do in Rust.

examples.title: Async & select
examples.text: async functions, .await, join and select are part of the language, not a library bolted on.

examples.title: Dynamic objects
examples.text: Objects, vectors and tuples are built in, so scripts can shape data as they go. They convert to and from Rust with serde.

examples.title: Compile-time constants
examples.text: A constant can be computed by running code in the compiler, so the work is done once rather than every call.

safeguards.title: Go ahead, try to hang it.
safeguards.text: Every script on this site runs with a budget of a million instructions, so this endless loop stops with an error instead of freezing the page. The budget is one of several limits a host sets around a script.

points.title: Instruction budgets
points.text: A host decides how many instructions a script may run. Native functions which loop draw from the same budget, so calling into Rust does not escape it.

points.title: Memory limits
points.text: Everything the language allocates goes through fallible collections, so a host can cap the memory a script uses while it is compiled and while it runs.

points.title: A bounded compiler
points.text: Nesting depth, macro expansion and constant evaluation each have a limit, so a source file cannot make the compiler run away.

points.title: No stack overflows from data
points.text: Comparing, hashing, formatting and dropping deeply nested values either works without recursion or ends in an error, rather than overflowing the host's stack.

safeguards.note: The goal is for a host to be able to run code it does not trust. Rune is not there yet: a limit holds only where the native functions a host exposes cooperate with it, so those still need vetting, and these safeguards are younger than the rest of the language.

embed.title: A few lines of Rust.
embed.text: Install the modules you want scripts to see, compile a script, and call into it. Native functions are plain Rust closures, and values cross the boundary with rune::from_value and rune::to_value.
embed.code:
use rune::{Context, Module, Source, Sources};

let mut module = Module::new();
module.function("greet", |name: String| format!("Hello, {name}!")).build()?;

let mut context = Context::with_default_modules()?;
context.install(module)?;

let mut sources = Sources::new();
sources.insert(Source::memory("pub fn main(user) { greet(user) }")?)?;

let mut vm = rune::prepare(&mut sources)
    .with_context(&context)
    .build_vm()?;

let output: String = rune::from_value(vm.call(["main"], ("Ferris",))?)?;
assert_eq!(output, "Hello, Ferris!");
